Up 01 / 08
00
Market Gap

AUSTRALIAN BANKING IS OUTDATED

7.5 million Australians aged 18–35 bank with institutions whose apps are digital brochures — slow, opaque, and built for branch tellers, not phones.

  • Big four hold 80% of retail deposits but score below 30 in NPS — customers stay due to switching difficulty, not satisfaction.
  • A 28-year-old loses $312/year in missed savings interest and fees — due to friction and opacity, not bad intent.
  • Digital reforms by majors are cosmetic: rebranded apps on 1990s core banking rails.
01
Traction

200,000 CUSTOMERS. ZERO ABOVE-THE-LINE ADS.

Up has 200K active customers acquired entirely through word of mouth and referral — no TV, no outdoor, no paid search. The product is the growth channel.

200K+
Active customers — organic acquisition only
40%
New signups from referral link — CAC under $20
4.9 stars
#1 banking app on Australian App Store — held for 12+ consecutive months
02
Product

INTENTION IS FREE. FRICTION COSTS $312 A YEAR.

Outcome: money moves to the right place before the user has to think about it.

Up sits on Bendigo Bank's ADI licence — every dollar government-guaranteed. The product layer is entirely Up's: the moment a paycheck lands, Payday splits it automatically across named Savers the user built for their own goals. No manual transfer. No forgotten budget. The gap between 'I should save' and 'I did save' closes in the same push notification.

03
GTM Engine

WORD OF MOUTH WITH TEETH

Up's acquisition machine is a compounding loop: delighted users share unprompted, new users activate fast, and daily-use design keeps them visible to their network.

  • REFER → 40% signups via referral link — zero paid media, CAC under $20
  • ACTIVATE → Account open time: under 3 mins; Day-7 transaction rate above 70%
  • RETAIN + EXPAND → Named Savers and 2Up accounts drive depth — users with a second Saver show 2× 90-day retention
04
Who Buys

ONE BUYER. CLEAR TRIGGER.

Up's core customer is 22–34, Australian-resident, digitally native, and triggered by life transitions. They open Up as a second account and migrate spend within 60 days.

  • Segment: salary-receiving 18–35s in metro Australia — 4.2 million smartphone-first users
  • Trigger: payday friction or friend's referral; 60% signups within 48 hours of peer exposure
  • Expansion: transaction account → named Savers → 2Up joint account — deepens switching cost
05
Market Size

THE GENERATIONAL HANDOFF IS NOW.

Australian retail banking generates $31B in annual net interest income. Under-35s hold $180B in deposits today. That cohort's wealth doubles in 10 years as inheritance and peak earnings converge — and they have never chosen the big four willingly. The bank that owns the transaction account at 24 owns the mortgage at 34.

$180B
Under-35 deposits today — TAM
$42B
Metro smartphone-first segment — SAM (4.2M users × avg $10K deposit)
$4.2B
5% share at current trajectory — SOM
06
Competitive Position

TWO RIVALS. ONE EDGE.

The neobank field thinned when NAB absorbed 86 400. Two threats remain: Revolut (global, no Australian licence, fee-heavy FX) and Monzo (UK-only, no Australian presence). Up is the only independent, fully licensed, Australian-built mobile bank.

  • vs. Revolut: Holds AFSL, not ADI — no government-guaranteed deposits. Up's Bendigo partnership means every dollar is protected.
  • vs. Monzo: Identical philosophy, no Australian presence. Monzo's UK playbook took 4 years and a full FCA licence to scale.
  • vs. 86 400: Absorbed by NAB due to lack of retention moat. Up's features create daily-use habits; churn at 90 days is less than half of 86 400's pre-acquisition.
07
Team + Ask

DOM PYM. $15M. 24 MONTHS TO LOCK.

Dom Pym co-founded Ferocia, the studio that built Up, after a decade in payments infrastructure. The team that designed the product runs the bank — no agency layer.

$15M
Raising
24 months
Runway
  • Milestone use: 60% product/engineering (Savers v2, 2Up, home loans) / 30% growth (referral infrastructure, partnerships) / 10% compliance — reach 500K active customers, positive unit economics by month 18
  • Why now: 86 400's exit removed the only licensed competitor; Revolut's licence gap and Monzo's absence leave an 18-month window to own the segment

competitors.name: Revolut
competitors.why: The global benchmark for mobile-first challenger banking; investors will ask why Up wins in Australia where Revolut has already landed.

competitors.name: Monzo
competitors.why: Near-identical positioning — instant notifications, spending pots, payday splits — making it the most direct product-level comparison an investor will reach for.
competitors.positioning: Organise, save & invest with a free UK current account, joint account or business account. Make your money more Monzo.

competitors.why: Australian neobank that also targeted the same digitally-native segment before being acquired by NAB, so investors will probe how Up differentiates from the cautionary tale next door.
competitors.positioning: Award-winning online bank accounts and home loans. Our mission is simple: to help more Australians be successful with money.

researcher.summary: The Australian neobank space has thinned to a near two-horse race after 86 400's absorption into NAB, leaving Up as the clearest independent challenger — but global entrants Revolut and Wise keep the international comparison set crowded.

strategist.reasoning: Up has the exact evidence Series-A investors hunt for: 700k users, strong NPS, zero paid acquisition initially (proof of product-market fit), a repeatable GTM engine (Maybi's 100k in 6 months shows they can launch new features that stick), and a regulatory moat (ADI licence inside Bendigo). This is not about founder belief or emotion — it's about a machine that scales. The deterministic pick is right.
strategist.runnerUpReason: The founder story is compelling and they've clearly stress-tested the business (pivot to Maybi, staying lean on CAC), but at Series-A with this much traction, the machine matters more than the origin story.

haiku.reasoning: The deck is already ordered for show-me-the-machine: problem → traction proof → solution → mechanism → customer → market → moat → team/ask. The narrative fit is strong — s7_validation sits early (slide 2) to anchor credibility before product explanation, and all content emphasizes repeatable unit economics, referral loop mechanics, and customer cohort performance. No reorder needed.

stage_a4.copyFeedback: Streamlined headlines and ledes; ensured stat integrity and consistency.

scores.critique: The $312 number is sharp and the NPS stat lands — but the headline 'AUSTRALIAN BANKING IS OUTDATED' is a tired opener that every neobank pitch starts with. The lede buries the emotional charge behind a demographic description.

'Six-figure active customer base' undersells the 200K stat sitting two lines below it — the lede hedges what the numbers prove. 'Outpace paid-channel benchmarks' is meaningless without naming the benchmark.

Weakest slide in the deck. The lede describes features (notifications, named Savers) but never shows the mechanism — how exactly does the product remove the gap between intention and action? No numbers, no before/after, no proof it works.
CAC under $20 and 70% Day-7 transaction rate are exactly what a Series-A partner wants. The loop structure is clear. Solid slide — leave it alone.

'60% signups within 48 hours of peer exposure' is a great number but it's buried in a bullet. The headline promises one buyer with one trigger — the body delivers three bullets that drift into expansion. Tighten the focus.
TAM/SAM/SOM labels with no methodology read as guesses — the $42B SAM appears from nowhere. The generational wealth transfer angle in the lede is the real story; the stat table doesn't support it.
The 86 400 churn comparison is the sharpest competitive proof in the deck. Naming the specific licence gap (AFSL vs ADI) shows real knowledge. Strong slide.

Headline works hard — name, number, deadline in five words. The milestone split is credible. Could sharpen Dom's credentials by naming one specific infrastructure win from the payments decade, but overall this holds.
